prompt.context: Our client, AirChief, is a small industrial company in Kansas, USA that manufactures aircraft maintenance and repair equipment. Their clients include (1) commercial airlines and (2) maintenance companies which airlines outsource aircraft maintenance to. AirChief has developed a proprietary chemical technology that allows airlines to repair lightning strike damage much faster than they currently can. They want to know whether they should commercialize said technology.
prompt.question: Should AirChief commercialize their new chemical lightning strike repair technology?

clarifying_info.q: Does AirChief plan to manufacture the product themselves or license the technology?
clarifying_info.a: AirChief is heavily vertically integrated and intends to manufacture the product themselves.

clarifying_info.q: What is AirChief's market position in lightning strike repair today?
clarifying_info.a: AirChief is one of two suppliers that sells the vast majority of specialized equipment for repairing aircraft, including the leading current lightning strike repair solution (although all current solutions are vastly similar).

clarifying_info.q: What is AirChief's goal with this technology?
clarifying_info.a: AirChief's goal is to achieve a profit by selling the technology they have developed.
AirChief operates solely in the United States.

clarifying_info.q: How important is lightning strike repair to AirChief's overall business?
clarifying_info.a: Lightning strike repair products are a small part of their overall catalog (think 4–6% revenue). As a result they are willing to wait a long time (5+ years) to see returns from a truly revolutionary product in the space.

clarifying_info.q: How does the current lightning strike repair process work?
clarifying_info.a: Lightning strikes typically cause small burns on the fuselage about the diameter of a shot glass. The damaged area must be placed under vacuum pressure and heated according to a set temperature/time curve to precisely activate a heat-sensitive adhesive. Currently, technicians must set up and program a complex heating device and microcontroller, in addition to making a one-use vacuum bag — both are time-consuming. If the temperature/time curve is not met, the repair must be redone.

clarifying_info.q: How does the new technology work?
clarifying_info.a: AirChief's innovation is a premade, reusable vacuum bag containing a pouch with two chemicals that, when mixed, consistently generates exactly the heating the adhesive requires (exothermic reaction). Technicians simply install the bag over the repair, break a seal to mix the chemicals, and walk away. The chemical reaction's predictability eliminates the risk of a failed repair.

framework: Market size: How large is the market? How many lightning strike repairs occur per year in the US?
Value proposition to customer / pricing: How compelling is the technology to end customers (airlines)? What impact does it have on their operations? How much would customers be willing to pay?
Cost to AirChief: What fixed and variable costs must AirChief incur to manufacture and sell the product?
Risks: Could this cannibalize AirChief's existing products? What competitive responses should be anticipated?
Alternative structure: Revenues and Costs to AirChief, with the above points mapped into Revenue (market size × price) and Cost (fixed setup + variable unit cost) buckets.

questions.prompt: Market sizing: How would you determine the number of lightning strike repairs this technology could serve per year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the key drivers: number of commercial flights per day in the US, probability of a lightning strike, and whether one strike causes one or two burn points. Work toward a total annual repairs figure. Strong candidates will ask what data is available rather than guessing.

math.setup: Start with daily US commercial flights, apply the lightning strike rate, then account for the fact that 1/3 of strikes produce two burn points (entry + exit) and 2/3 produce only one.
steps: Daily lightning strikes: 3,000 flights/day × 0.1% struck = 3 lightning strikes/day
Total burn repairs per day: 2 (from double-burn) + 2 (from single-burn) = 4 repairs/day
math.answer: Approximately 1,400 lightning strike repairs needed per year in the US.

questions.prompt: Value proposition: Why might an airline prefer AirChief's new technology, and can you quantify the value of the time it saves?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first brainstorm qualitative benefits (faster repair, more reliable outcome, eliminates one-use vacuum bag cost, saves technician labor, more environmentally friendly). Then, when directed, quantify the value of the 3-hour time saving. The key insight is that repairs currently take 8 hours; the new tech takes 5 hours — a 3-hour saving. Airlines fly 6am–midnight (18 operating hours). Lightning repairs are done overnight; airlines may fly for up to 24 hours before repairing. The new tech allows 2 additional hours of flight at either the start or end of the day. Candidate should calculate the margin on those 2 extra hours of flying.

math.setup: Calculate the profit an airline earns from flying a plane for 2 additional hours (avoided lost revenue). Use: seats × load factor = passengers; passengers × ticket price per flight hour × hours = revenue; revenue × margin = profit.
steps: Passengers on a typical 737/A320: 150 seats × 80% load factor = 120 passengers
Revenue from 2 extra hours: 120 passengers × $50/flight hour × 2 hours = $12,000
Profit retained: $12,000 × 7.5% margin = $900 per repair event
math.answer: Each use of the new technology is worth approximately $900 in incremental profit to the airline (from avoided missed ticket revenue). This is the baseline willingness-to-pay floor — the true value is higher once flight disruption costs are considered.

questions.prompt: Costs: What costs would AirChief incur to bring this product to market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish fixed (one-time setup) costs from variable (per-unit) costs. With the market size (1,400 units/year) and the value figure from the prior step, candidate should check whether the business case is positive or negative at the unit cost and market size determined.

math.setup: Fixed costs = regulatory approvals + manufacturing equipment. Variable cost = per-unit production cost. Compare unit economics against willingness-to-pay.
steps: At $900 value per repair, the unit cost ($1,200) exceeds the quantified value ($900), suggesting the basic business case is negative at that price point — unless additional value drivers (disruption costs) justify a higher price.
math.answer: Unit cost of $1,200 exceeds the $900 quantified benefit at the baseline; the full value proposition (including disruption avoidance) must be explored to justify a price above cost.

brainstorming.prompt: Can you think of any reasons AirChief may be able to command a higher price than the $900 we calculated — reasons our analysis so far has not covered?

categories.name: Airline flight disruption costs
ideas: When a plane is unavailable for 2+ hours, it disrupts a tightly coordinated flight network
Missed connections and passenger rerouting costs
Potential financial compensation for cancelled or delayed flights
Airport slot penalties or fees for schedule violations

categories.name: Brand and customer experience
ideas: Airline brand reputation damage from unexpected delays
Customer goodwill and loyalty impact from disruptions
Social media / PR exposure from publicised cancellations

categories.name: Operational reliability
ideas: More predictable repair outcome (no need to redo a failed repair) reduces downtime risk further
Reusable vacuum bag reduces consumable costs airlines currently bear
Reduced technician training time and error rate
Fewer repair failures means fewer aircraft out of service unexpectedly

categories.name: Competitive positioning
ideas: Technology may be patentable, creating a pricing moat
Airlines may pay a premium for a sole-source supplier of a superior product
Long-term supply contracts at premium pricing become feasible

recommendation: We recommend that AirChief commercialize the chemical heating vacuum bag for lightning strike repairs.

After studying airlines' operations, we believe airlines would be willing to pay a sum far exceeding the product's unit cost once the full value is quantified — specifically the value of avoiding flight schedule disruptions entirely.

The 3-hour repair time saving allows airlines to fully repair lightning strike damage within regular overnight pauses, eliminating the risk of a plane being pulled from service and causing network disruptions. That disruption avoidance value almost certainly dwarfs the $900 baseline revenue figure.
Given AirChief's existing market position as one of two dominant suppliers of aircraft repair equipment, they are well placed to sell this product into their existing customer base.
risks: Unit cost ($1,200) exceeds the quantified per-use revenue benefit ($900) at baseline pricing — final pricing must be anchored to full disruption cost data, not just missed ticket revenue.
Potential cannibalization of AirChief's existing lightning strike repair product line (currently ~4–6% of revenue).
Competitive response from the other dominant supplier, who may develop a competing solution.
Regulatory approval process adds $250,000 in fixed costs and timeline uncertainty.
Market is small (~1,400 repairs/year); revenue upside is limited unless pricing is set well above unit cost.
next_steps: Conduct detailed analysis of the cost of airline flight network disruptions per event to properly anchor the product's price.
Evaluate IP protection and patent filing options to defend the technology.
Engage with 2–3 key airline customers for pricing discovery conversations.
Allocate space in the new Alabama plant to begin production ramp, contingent on pricing analysis confirming positive unit economics.
